title: Repository Security & Access Guidelines
body: Repository Security & Access Guidelines Quick Jumps Overview Access Control Curriculum Repository (git-going-with-github) Student Repositories (created by GitHub Classroom) Organization Membership Branch Protection Curriculum Repository (main branch) Student Repositories What Students Cannot Do Permission Model Least Privilege Facilitator Access Required Access Level Adding a Facilitator Removing a Facilitator After the Workshop GitHub Actions Security Workflows in Student Repositories Curriculum Repository Workflows Data Privacy What Data Is Stored What Data Is NOT Stored Data Retention Safety Checks Before the Workshop During the Workshop Rollback & Emergency If Something Goes Wrong Compliance & Audit What Is Logged Audit Priorities Contact & Support Authoritative Sources Section-Level Source Map Overview This repository hosts the curriculum and facilitator materials for the Git Going with GitHub workshop. Student work happens in individual private repositories created by GitHub Classroom, not in this repository. This document covers the security model for both the curriculum repository and the student repositories. Access Control Curriculum Repository (git-going-with-github) Role Repository Issues PRs Settings Facilitators Full access Full access Review and merge Admin Contributors Read Create and comment Create None Public Read View View None This repository is public. It contains no secrets, student data, or sensitive configuration. All curriculum content is openly licensed. Student Repositories (created by GitHub Classroom) Role Repository Issues PRs Settings Student (owner) Read/Write Full access Create and merge Limited (no Actions config) Facilitators Full access via Classroom Full access Review and comment Admin Other students No access No access No access No access Student repositories are private by default . Each student can only see their own repo. Facilitators see all student repos through the GitHub Classroom dashboard. Organization Membership Students do not need to be members of the Community-Access organization. GitHub Classroom handles all access automatically when a student accepts an assignment invite link. The student is granted access to their individual repo without any org-level permissions. Facilitators do need organization-level access to manage the classroom. See the Facilitator Access section below. Branch Protection Curriculum Repository (main branch) Protection Rules: Require pull request reviews: Yes (1 approval minimum) Require status checks to pass: Yes (GitHub Actions validation) Require branches to be up to date: No (to avoid unnecessary merge conflicts) Allow auto-merge: No (manual merge only for safety) Allow force pushes: No (protect history) Allow deletions: No (protect branch) Student Repositories Student repos are created from the learning-room-template . Branch protection in student repos is intentionally minimal: Students can create branches freely (required for challenges) Students can merge their own PRs (required for the learning flow) No force push protection (students are learning; mistakes are part of the process) GitHub Actions workflows run with read/write permissions (required for Gandalf and the Progression Bot) What Students Cannot Do Even within their own repo, students cannot: Access GitHub Actions secrets at the organization level Modify workflow files that run with elevated permissions Access other students' repositories View the classroom admin settings Permission Model Least Privilege The GitHub Classroom model enforces least privilege by design: Students are not organization members Students have no access to the curriculum repository's settings Students have no access to other students' repos Students have no access to CI/CD secrets or org-level configuration Students can create branches, issues, and PRs in their own repo Students can push to any branch in their own repo Students can merge PRs in their own repo (with autograder checks reporting status) Facilitator Access Required Access Level Facilitators must be Owners or Admins of the Community-Access organization to: Create and manage GitHub Classroom assignments View all student repositories through the classroom dashboard Comment on student PRs via the feedback pull request Monitor autograding results Troubleshoot workflow failures in student repos Adding a Facilitator # Add a facilitator as an org admin gh api /orgs/Community-Access/memberships/USERNAME -X PUT -f role=admin # Verify the role gh api /orgs/Community-Access/memberships/USERNAME --jq .role # Expected output: "admin" Removing a Facilitator After the Workshop # Downgrade to member (retains read access) or remove entirely gh api /orgs/Community-Access/memberships/USERNAME -X DELETE GitHub Actions Security Workflows in Student Repositories The template repository includes these workflows, which are copied into every student repo: Workflow Trigger Permissions What It Does pr-validation-bot.yml PR opened/u

body: VibeVoice Voice Comparison Setup Quick Jumps Hear samples right now -- no install required Available built-in English voices Experimental voice packs (run `demo/download_experimental_voices.sh`) Local setup (Windows, NVIDIA GPU recommended) Prerequisites Step 1: Run the setup script Step 2: Generate comparison samples Manual usage (from inside the VibeVoice repo) Python script options Model notes Tools for evaluating and comparing Microsoft VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B voices before choosing one for your project. License: Research/development use only (MIT). Not for commercial production. Every generated audio file includes an audible "This segment was generated by AI" disclaimer embedded automatically by the model. Hear samples right now -- no install required Option URL Notes HuggingFace Space https://huggingface.co/spaces/anycoderapps/VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B Free, browser-based, pick voice and enter text Project demo page https://microsoft.github.io/VibeVoice/ Pre-rendered podcast-length audio with named speakers Google Colab https://colab.research.google.com/github/microsoft/VibeVoice/blob/main/demo/vibevoice_realtime_colab.ipynb Free GPU via Colab, full control Available built-in English voices These ship with the repo -- no extra downloads needed. Voice key Gender Character en-Carter_man Male Neutral American, clear diction en-Davis_man Male Warm American, slightly slower cadence en-Emma_woman Female Clear American, professional tone en-Frank_man Male Deeper resonance, authoritative en-Grace_woman Female Softer delivery, friendly en-Mike_man Male Conversational, natural pace in-Samuel_man Male Indian-English accent, distinct character Experimental voice packs (run demo/download_experimental_voices.sh ) After downloading, 11 additional English style variants are available plus voices for German, French, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, Polish, Portuguese, and Spanish. Local setup (Windows, NVIDIA GPU recommended) Prerequisites Windows 10/11 with an NVIDIA GPU (RTX 3060+ recommended for real-time) Python 3.10 or later: https://www.python.org/downloads/ Git: https://git-scm.com/download/win NVIDIA CUDA 11.8 or 12.x drivers Step 1: Run the setup script scripts\vibevoice\setup-vibevoice.bat This will: Create a Python virtual environment ( vibevoice-env\ ) Install PyTorch with CUDA support Clone microsoft/VibeVoice into VibeVoice\ Install the VibeVoice streaming TTS package Step 2: Generate comparison samples scripts\vibevoice\generate-voice-samples.bat This generates one WAV file per voice in VibeVoice\voice-samples\ using the same comparison sentence so the voices are directly comparable. A README.md with a voice summary table is written alongside the WAV files. Manual usage (from inside the VibeVoice repo) REM Activate the venv first vibevoice-env\Scripts\activate.bat cd VibeVoice REM Single voice python demo\realtime_model_inference_from_file.py ^ --model_path microsoft/VibeVoice-Realtime- 0 . 5 B ^ --txt_path demo\text_examples\ 1 p_vibevoice.txt ^ --speaker_name Carter REM Custom text (create a .txt file first) echo Your custom narration text here. > my_script.txt python demo\realtime_model_inference_from_file.py ^ --model_path microsoft/VibeVoice-Realtime- 0 . 5 B ^ --txt_path my_script.txt ^ --speaker_name Emma Output WAV files are saved to ./outputs/ by default. Python script options python generate-voice-samples.py [ options ] --model-path PATH HF model ID or local path (default: microsoft/VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B) --voices-dir PATH Path to demo/voices/streaming_model --output-dir PATH Where to save WAVs (default: ./voice-samples) --text "..." Override the comparison sentence --all-languages Include non-English voices (download required) --device cuda|mps|cpu Override auto-detected device Model notes Model: VibeVoice-Realtime-0.5B (single-speaker streaming TTS) Context: 8k tokens (~10 min audio) Latency: ~300ms first audio on NVIDIA T4 or Apple M4 Pro Multi-speaker: The multi-speaker TTS-1.5B model was removed from the repo in September 2025 due to misuse. Only Realtime-0.5B is currently available. Watermark: Every output includes an audible AI disclaimer and an imperceptible provenance watermark.

title: Security Policy
body: Security Policy Quick Jumps Supported Versions Reporting a Vulnerability Preferred Method - Private Vulnerability Reporting What to Report What Is Out of Scope Response Timeline Scope and Impact Credit Authoritative Sources Section-Level Source Map Supported Versions This repository contains educational curriculum and documentation only - no production software, application servers, or APIs. There are no versioned software releases to patch. Table: Supported content types and their source Content Supported Curriculum documentation (docs/) Current main branch GitHub Actions workflows (.github/workflows/) Current main branch Build scripts (scripts/) Current main branch AI agent prompts (.github/prompts/, .github/agents/) Current main branch Reporting a Vulnerability Please do not report security vulnerabilities as public GitHub Issues. Public issues are visible to everyone, including people who might exploit the vulnerability before it is fixed. Preferred Method - Private Vulnerability Reporting This repository has Private Vulnerability Reporting enabled. To submit a report: Navigate to the Security tab of this repository Select "Report a vulnerability" Fill in the form with: A clear title describing the issue A detailed description of the vulnerability and its potential impact Steps to reproduce (if applicable) Your suggested fix (optional but appreciated) Submit - only the maintainers will see your report What to Report Even though this is an educational repository, the following are genuine security concerns: Malicious content injected into curriculum files - documentation that contains links to phishing sites, malware downloads, or misleading instructions GitHub Actions workflow vulnerabilities - script injection risks in .github/workflows/ , insecure use of GITHUB_TOKEN , or pull-request-triggered workflows that execute untrusted code Hardcoded credentials - any real tokens, passwords, or API keys accidentally committed to any file Supply chain risks - compromised npm dependencies used by the build system Prompt injection in agent files - AI agent prompts ( .prompt.md , .agent.md ) that could manipulate an LLM to produce harmful output What Is Out of Scope Theoretical attacks with no realistic exploitation path Vulnerabilities in GitHub's own infrastructure (report those to GitHub directly at the GitHub Security page ) Broken links or outdated documentation (open a regular issue for those) Response Timeline Milestone Target Acknowledge receipt Within 3 business days Initial assessment Within 7 business days Fix deployed (if confirmed) Within 30 days for critical/high; 90 days for medium/low Public disclosure After fix is deployed, or coordinated with reporter Scope and Impact This curriculum is designed to teach GitHub to workshop participants. The primary security risks are: Documentation accuracy - incorrect instructions that could cause participants to configure their systems insecurely Workflow integrity - GitHub Actions that run on pull requests from forks require careful scoping to prevent privilege escalation Dependency security - the build system uses Node.js packages that must be kept up to date Credit Security researchers who responsibly disclose valid vulnerabilities will be credited in the repository's release notes (unless they prefer to remain anonymous). For general questions about the curriculum, open a regular issue. For security concerns, use private reporting above. Explore Git History Visually Suggested order Consolidated walkthrough of the 21 issue-based challenges in the Learning Room. Use this as a single working file while you move through the challenge issues in order. Core challenges 1. Find Your Way Around Chapter links: Ch02, Ch03, Ch04 Goal: Explore the repository, find the Issues tab, and locate key files. Do: Find the Code tab and count files in the repository root. Open Issues and find an open issue. Read the first paragraph of docs/welcome.md . Find the repository description and the README. Evidence: Short notes about what you found in each step. 2. File Your First Issue Chapter link: Ch05 Goal: Find a TODO in docs/welcome.md and turn it into a clear issue. Do: Search docs/welcome.md for TODO . Open a new issue with a specific title. Explain what needs to change, where it is, and why it matters. Evidence: Link to the issue you created and explain the TODO. 3. Join the Conversation Chapter links: Ch05, Ch08 Goal: Practice comments, @mentions, and reactions in an issue thread. Do: Find the peer-simulation issue or a buddy issue. Leave a useful comment with an @mention. Add a reaction or another helpful response. Evidence: Link to your comment and describe why it was useful. 4. Branch Out Chapter links: Ch06, Ch04 Goal: Create a safe working branch for your Day 1 changes. Do: Find the branch selector. Create learn/YOUR-USERNAME from main . Confirm you are on the new branch. Evidence: Branch name and how you confirmed it. 5. Make Your Mark Chapter links: Ch06, Ch04 Goal: Edit docs/welcome.md and commit the change clearly. Do: Switch to learn/YOUR-USERNAME . Replace the TODO in docs/welcome.md . Commit with a meaningful message. Evidence: Commit message and edited file. 6. Open Your First Pull Request Chapter link: Ch06 Goal: Open a PR from your branch to main . Do: Create a pull request from learn/YOUR-USERNAME to main . Include Closes #XX in the description. Write a clear title and summary. Evidence: PR link and the issue it closes. 7. Survive a Merge Conflict Chapter link: Ch07 Goal: Resolve a merge conflict safely and cleanly. Do: Wait for the conflict to be triggered. Read the conflict markers carefully. Keep the right content and delete all marker lines. Commit the resolution. Evidence: What you kept and why. 8. The Culture Layer Chapter links: Ch08, Ch09 Goal: Reflect on open source culture and practice issue triage. Do: Answer the reflection prompt. Add or recommend a label if the issue asks for triage. Explain your communication or triage choice. Evidence: Three concrete collaboration behaviors you will use. 9. Merge Day Chapter links: Ch06, Ch10 Goal: Merge your Day 1 PR and confirm the issue closes. Do: Verify the PR is ready. Merge it or have a facilitator merge it. Confirm the change landed on main . Confirm the linked issue closed automatically. Evidence: Merged PR link and closed issue number. 10. Go Local Chapter links: Ch13, Ch14 Goal: Clone the repo locally, work on a branch, commit, and push. Do: Clone the Learning Room repository. Create fix/YOUR-USERNAME . Edit a file in docs/ . Commit and push the branch to GitHub. Evidence: Branch name and how you confirmed the push. 11. Open a Day 2 PR Chapter links: Ch14, Ch15 Goal: Open a PR from a locally pushed branch. Do: Open a PR from fix/YOUR-USERNAME to main . Write a clear title and description. Confirm the branch-to-main workflow feels familiar. Evidence: PR link and what changed. 12. Review Like a Pro Chapter link: Ch15 Goal: Give thoughtful code review feedback. Do: Open a buddy PR or peer-simulation PR. Read the diff in Files changed. Leave at least two inline comments. Submit a review verdict. Evidence: Review link or where the comments were left. 13. AI as Your Copilot Chapter link: Ch16 Goal: Use Copilot as a collaborator, then judge its suggestions. Do: Ask Copilot to improve a documentation file. Accept, modify, or reject suggestions thoughtfully. Keep notes on what changed and why. Evidence: Prompt used and one suggestion you changed or rejected. 14. Template Remix Chapter link: Ch17 Goal: Create an accessible YAML issue template.
